**S-corp election on an LLC is usually smarter at ~$180k** for a consulting business, but it depends on your specifics.

### Quick breakdown
- **LLC** (default): Simple. All net profit gets hit with self-employment tax (~15.3% on top of income tax). Easy bookkeeping, no payroll required.
- **S-corp** (tax election you can make on an LLC): You pay yourself a “reasonable salary” (payroll taxes on that), and the remaining profit comes out as distributions **not** subject to self-employment tax. That SE tax savings is the main win.

### At $180k revenue
Assuming decent margins (consulting often has high ones after expenses):
- SE tax savings can easily be $8–15k+/year once you get past the salary.
- You must run payroll, file extra forms (1120S, K-1, payroll returns), and keep a reasonable salary (IRS looks at this—too low and they can reclassify).
- Extra costs: payroll service (~$50–100/mo), possibly a bit more accounting.

**Rough rule of thumb**: S-corp often starts making sense around $80–100k+ net profit. At $180k gross you’re probably in the worthwhile zone if your expenses aren’t huge.

### What I’d do
1. Form an LLC (or keep it if you already have one) for liability protection + flexibility.
2. Elect S-corp taxation (Form 2553) once numbers justify the admin.
3. Talk to a CPA who knows small consulting businesses—they’ll run the actual numbers on your expenses, state rules, retirement contributions, etc. This is not advice; tax situations vary a lot (especially by state).

ok so s-corp it is. how do i elect that. like what's the form

**Form 2553** — “Election by a Small Business Corporation.”

### Quick steps
1. Make sure your LLC (or corp) qualifies: US shareholders only, ≤100 shareholders, one class of stock, eligible entity, etc.
2. Fill out **Form 2553**. You’ll need consent/signatures from all shareholders/members.
3. File it with the IRS (mailing address depends on your location — check the form instructions).
4. **Timing matters**:
   - To be effective for the current tax year → generally file by March 15 of that year (or within 2 months 15 days of formation if new).
   - You can also file late in some cases with reasonable-cause relief, but don’t count on it.

Most people have their CPA or tax pro handle the form + the reasonable salary setup + payroll. It’s short but easy to mess up the effective date or eligibility.

filed the 2553 myself last year so i can do that part. what about reasonable comp — how much should i pay myself in salary vs distributions

**There’s no official IRS percentage or formula** — “reasonable compensation” is whatever a similar business would pay someone to do your job. Get this wrong (especially too low) and the IRS can reclassify distributions as wages + hit you with back payroll taxes, penalties, and interest.

### How the IRS looks at it
They consider things like:
- Your duties, skills, experience, and time spent
- What comparable companies pay for similar roles in your area
- Your business’s revenue, profits, and payments to non-shareholder employees
- Industry norms

For a consulting business where you’re basically the whole show, salary usually needs to look like a real market wage for that work — not a token amount so you can stuff everything into distributions.

### Practical ways people set it
1. **Market rate approach (strongest)**: Look up what an employee consultant/owner-operator with your experience would earn in your metro/industry (BLS, Glassdoor, salary.com, industry surveys). Pay yourself at least that for the work you actually do.
2. **Common rules of thumb** (not law, just starting points people + CPAs use):  
   - Often 30–50%+ of net profit as salary (varies widely)  
   - Or enough salary to max certain payroll-tax / retirement benefits you care about  
   At ~$180k revenue, once you subtract real business expenses, many solo consultants end up with salary in a broad six-figure-ish range if they’re full-time and doing billable work — but it depends entirely on your net profit, hours, and local rates.
3. Document it: keep notes on how you picked the number (salary comps, etc.). Helps if you’re ever questioned.

### Important realities
- You must run actual payroll (withholdings, payroll taxes, W-2, etc.). Distributions are separate and don’t get SE/payroll tax.
- Too low = audit risk. Too high = you lose some of the SE-tax savings that made S-corp worth it.
- State rules and your specific facts (other employees? multiple shareholders? home office? retirement plan?) change the math.

**Bottom line**: A good CPA or tax pro who does S-corps for consultants should run the numbers on *your* profit, role, and location and help set/document the salary. This is one of the spots where DIY gets expensive if the IRS disagrees. Since you already filed the 2553, the next move is usually getting payroll set up and locking in that reasonable salary figure with professional input.

What’s your rough net profit after expenses (or typical margins)? And are you solo full-time? That narrows the ballpark.

**Got it — but slow down a notch before you lock 80k / 100k in tomorrow.**

That split can be perfectly fine for some solo consultants at ~$180k revenue, or it can be too light on salary depending on your actual net profit, hours, role, location, and market rates. The IRS doesn’t care what a chat suggested; they care whether the salary is defensible as reasonable compensation for the work you do. If expenses are low and you’re the whole business, they often expect the salary to look more like a real market wage for a full-time consultant with your skills.

### Quick reality checks
- **Net profit matters more than revenue.** 80k salary + 100k distributions assumes roughly $180k left after expenses (or that you’re distributing almost everything). Run the real numbers after business deductions.
- **Document why 80k is reasonable** — comps for similar roles in your area, your duties/time, etc. “Someone on the internet said it was cool” won’t help in an audit.
- **Payroll has to be real.** You can’t just journal it. Need actual withholdings, deposits, payroll filings, W-2, etc. Most people use a service (Gusto, etc.) once they’re an S-corp.
- Your old CPA’s “it depends” was annoying but directionally correct — this part is facts-and-circumstances.

I’m useful for the overview and the Form 2553 pointer; I’m not a substitute for a CPA/tax pro who can look at *your* P&L, state rules, and retirement plans and help you set + defend the number. Worth the fee so you don’t give the SE-tax savings back later in penalties.

If you want, tell me your rough annual expenses/net or your metro/industry and I can help you think through questions to ask a new CPA. Otherwise, smart next move is still a quick paid consult before you run payroll on that split. You’re in a good spot having the 2553 already done.

**Glad the overview helped — but don’t skip the CPA entirely.**

I can walk you through the big picture and forms at a high level. I can’t look at your actual books, state rules, exact net profit, retirement options, or defend your salary if the IRS ever asks. That’s where DIY S-corp stuff gets expensive.

### Things I’d still add / watch for
- **Payroll has to be real and on time.** Salary means withholdings, payroll tax deposits, quarterly filings (941), W-2 at year-end, unemployment, etc. Use a service (Gusto, ADP, etc.) — don’t try to DIY that part.
- **Reasonable comp documentation.** Keep a short file: how you picked $80k (salary comps, your role/hours, industry data). “Chat said it was fine” won’t cut it.
- **Quarterly estimated taxes.** You’ll still owe income tax on the distributions (and the salary). Don’t get surprised by underpayment penalties.
- **State stuff.** Some states tax S-corps differently, have their own filings, or don’t recognize the election the same way.
- **Bookkeeping cleanliness.** Separate business account, track every expense properly, and keep basis records. Distributions aren’t free money if you don’t have basis.
- **Retirement / benefits.** Solo 401k or similar can change the optimal salary vs distribution mix and save more tax than the S-corp election alone.
- **Year-end.** 1120S, K-1, payroll returns — easy to mess up deadlines or details.

Your old CPA charging $4k and just saying “it depends” sounds frustrating. A better one should actually run the numbers, help set the salary, and handle (or review) the filings for less drama. Even a one-time consult + payroll setup review this year is cheaper than penalties later.

You’re in a solid spot with the 2553 already done. If you want, I can help you make a short checklist of questions to ask a new CPA so you don’t get the vague treatment again. Otherwise the smartest add is still getting a pro to sanity-check the $80k/$100k split and payroll setup before you run with it.
